quotes.text: Renowned for blending the radical innovations of atonality and twelve-tone (dodecaphonic) techniques with rich Romantic lyricism and expressive intensity, Berg's music is marked by emotional depth, formal sophistication, and a deep connection to human drama.
While embracing Schoenberg's innovations, Berg infused his own music with lyrical warmth and emotional immediacy, setting him apart from his peers.
Berg's music maintained a connection to late-Romantic traditions (influences from Mahler and Wagner), while incorporating atonality and twelve-tone techniques.
He masterfully balanced expressive melody, rich harmonies, and formal rigor, making his avant-garde works more accessible to listeners unfamiliar with atonality.

Though Berg adopted Schoenberg's twelve-tone method, he was more flexible in his approach. He often blurred the boundaries between tonal and atonal music, allowing moments of emotional lyricism to shine through.
Berg's ability to merge emotional expressiveness with strict twelve-tone structures made his works more relatable and enduring.
The opera uses innovative techniques such as leitmotifs, symmetrical structures, and Sprechstimme to convey emotional turmoil.
The opera employs a complex twelve-tone structure while maintaining emotional intensity and dramatic clarity.
The piece fuses twelve-tone technique with a hauntingly lyrical quality, including a quotation of a Bach chorale that imbues the work with a sense of transcendence.
Berg's music, while deeply modern, remained more accessible to wider audiences due to its emotional resonance and connection to Romantic traditions.
Berg's ability to integrate emotional expression with serial techniques inspired many later composers to explore twelve-tone methods in a more flexible and expressive manner.
His unique synthesis of tradition and innovation remains a hallmark of 20th-century music.
Alban Berg's journey was one of remarkable transformation—an evolution from a self-taught young romantic into a pioneering modernist whose works shaped the course of 20th-century music.
His life, though tragically short, was filled with artistic exploration, deep emotional expression, and a constant search for balance between tradition and innovation.
Berg wrote atonal and 12-tone compositions that remained true to late 19th-century Romanticism.
The musical precepts and the human example provided by Schoenberg shaped Berg's artistic personality as they worked together for the next six years.

A characteristic of Berg's creative activity was the slow, often hesitant, manner in which he gave final form to the musical ideas that, for the most part, were the result of sudden inspiration. This fastidious, perfectionist manner of composing explains his relatively small number of works.
The sometimes erotic postcard texts were sufficiently nonconformist to prompt Berg to use them as background for even less traditional music than he had composed in the past.

Wozzeck represents Berg's first attempt to deal with social problems within the framework of opera. From numerous statements he made, it is evident that he intended the opera to portray far more than the tragic fate of the protagonist. He wanted, in fact, to make it symbolic of human existence.

Musically, its unity stems from large overall symmetries within which are set traditional forms (such as the passacaglia and sonata), excerpts in popular music style, dense chromaticism, extreme atonality, and passing approaches to traditional tonality, all of which function to create a work of notable psychological and dramatic impact.
Berg had also become an outstanding teacher of composition.
it's striking to hear such a potent elucidation of Mahler's influence on Berg's style.
